Part I — Knowledge Base (English)
Bhaiya's Teachings — Knowledge Base (Session 24)
Topic: Maan-Samman (Honor) Is the Ultimate Addiction — Why "Pitching" Any Quality Invites Your Own Downfall, and the Mahasukshma Sharir Behind Every Sankalp

Sour ce: A live Ashaeiynn sangat satsang (video transcript, ~1 hour 19 minutes) — a genuine back-and-forth session with extensive live audience participation, questions, pushback, and confirmations, not a solo training monologue. Purpose: Chatbot knowledge — English version. Note on conversational content: this session contains substantial live sangat interaction — see the separate Hinglish conversational supplement (Part III) for curated exchanges.
1. WHY THIS TOPIC MATTERS

This session opens with a dir ect question to the sangat: what is the single biggest nasha (addiction/intoxication) a person can have? Candidate answers from the audience — vasana (desire), alcohol, fame, power — are each considered and set aside. The answer given is maan-samman-izzat: honor , respect, and r eputation. This teaching ar gues that this specific addiction is powerful enough to consume even the greatest of saints (" बड़े से बड़े संत को कच्चा खा जाता है").
2. WHY HONOR OUTLASTS EVERY OTHER ADDICTION

A recognizable, r elatable example is used to make the point concr ete: elderly par ents (50+, 60+, even 70+) who have let go of many attachments over a lifetime, but who still cling tightly to one thing until the very end — "log kya kahenge" (what will people say). This is of fered as proof that the addiction to reputation outlasts nearly every other attachment. People ar e able to over come vasana (desir e). People ar e able to over come dietary r estrictions and food attachments. People ar e even able to give up wealth. But people ar e almost never able to let go of their izzat (honor/r eputation) — being publicly insulted or shown up in front of others (" सबके सामने बेइज्जती") is described as one of the most painful experiences a person can have, more painful than most other losses.
3. THE CORE LAW: "JISKO PITCH KAROGE WAHI PINCH KAREGA"

The central teachable principle of this session: whatever quality or claim you loudly attach to your own identity and honor ("pitch" it), that exact same quality will eventually be used to strike you down ("pinch" you). The stated mechanism: shakti (power/spiritual for ce) always clashes with matching shakti — when a person's ego or public claim rises to touch a higher -level power , that higher power responds and brings the person down specifically through the very thing they staked their honor on. This is explicitly framed as a case-study exer cise, not gossip or moral judgment about any individual's personal life — the stated purpose is to understand the underlying mechanism (referred to in this session as Surya Vigyan, "Sun science"), not to take sides on any specific public figure's guilt or innocence.
4. CASE STUDY ONE: NITYANAND MAHARAJ — REAL SHAKTI, UNSHAKEN DESPITE ACCUSATIONS

Nityanand Maharaj is pr esented as a genuine practitioner: Shiv gan (Lord Shiva's attendant spirits) ar e described as present with him, he is described as a devotee of Sadashiva, and he is understood to have spent r oughly 20-25 years in serious sadhna in this field befor e his following gr ew large. Despite public accusations of being "charitraheen" (characterless) — the very first accusation levied against him — his following, r esour ces, and power ar e described as fundamentally undiminished: he purchased an entire island, established his own separate currency (bearing an image of Ram Setu), and continues to be recognized and engaged with even by foreign governments regarding travel. The teaching's point: because he never publicly staked his honor on a claim of purity , accusations on that fr ont could not actually dislodge his underlying power . Drug distribution is also mentioned as having r eportedly occurr ed at his institute without him ever being personally implicated or caught — the teaching's explanation is that he did not personally engage in it, so the shakti supporting him remained undisturbed; those who acted wrongly on their own initiative bear that consequence themselves, not him.
5. CASE STUDY TWO: BAGESHWAR SARKAR VS. PANDOKAR SARKAR — THE VULNERABILITY OF A PURITY CLAIM

Two contemporary babas ar e directly compar ed. Bageshwar Sarkar is described as r epeatedly , publicly insisting: "we don't even think about vasana, we only do upasana (worship)." This repeated public claim is the key detail examined. Pandokar Sarkar , by contrast, is described (per this teaching's account, via drishti) as having r oughly four times the shakti of Bageshwar Dham, with Hanuman Ji Maharaj himself said to work dir ectly thr ough him — and this individual has two marriages on record, with a third reportedly being considered, without ever having made a public claim of vasanafreedom. The teaching's conclusion: because Bageshwar Sarkar tied his own honor directly to a claim of vasana-purity , that specific claim becomes his single point of vulnerability — a single fabricated clip or rumor involving a woman could collapse his following entir ely , since the exposur e would dir ectly contradict the very thing his honor was staked on. Pandokar Sarkar , having never made that claim, has no equivalent vulnerability on that specific front — his following isn't shaken by his marital record, because he never claimed otherwise.
6. CASE STUDY THREE: OSHO AND SADHGURU — SAFETY THROUGH NEVER MAKING THE CLAIM

Osho is described as having openly told people to do what they wish and connect with God without excessive fear ar ound vasana — his well-known formulation "sambhog se samadhi" (fr om union to enlightenment) is cited as an example of never pitching sexual abstinence as part of his image. Because he never staked his honor on that claim, the teaching notes that "no one ever said anything to him" on that front. Similarly , Jaggi Vasudev (Sadhguru), founder of the Isha Foundation, is described as never having written or stated in his books or teachings that people should stay away fr om vasana. He is also described as freely mixing and socializing with people without ever appearing in scandal-driven news on this specific front — again, because he never pitched a purity claim, ther e was no specific vulnerability for that claim to be pinched thr ough.
7. THE GENERAL PATTERN ACROSS ALL FOUR CASE STUDIES

Across all four examples, the same underlying pattern holds: it is specifically the babas who r epeatedly and publicly insist "stay away fr om vasana" who eventually fall thr ough vasana-r elated scandal, while those who never made that

specific public claim do not experience that particular vulnerability , regardless of their actual personal conduct. The point being taught is not about which conduct is right or wrong — it is about the mechanism by which publicly staking honor on a specific claim cr eates a specific point of exposur e.
8. BHAGW AN SHIVA AS THE ULTIMATE EXAMPLE OF NEVER "PITCHING" ANYTHING

Lord Shiva is pr esented as the ultimate teacher on this principle, pr ecisely because he never attached his honor (izzat) to any single fact, quality , or claim about himself. Because nothing was ever "pitched," nothing could ever "pinch" him. This teaching r eferences material fr om what is described as the Shiv Purana's older material (r eferred to in this session as "Seven Secr ets of Shiva") stating that the seed/r oot of desir e (vasana) exists within Lord Shiva's own body , and that his wisdom lies specifically in never letting that particular element leave his body outward. It is said that when Bhagwan Shiva and Mata Parvati would go away together for six to seven months at a time, and sages/hermits later encountered them, Mata Parvati would cover her face in modesty — this detail is pr esented as self-evident in existing iconography and texts, not as speculation. Despite being associated with the most impur e company (per this teaching, spending time with ash, cr emation gr ounds, and unconventional company) and r eportedly also associated with cannabis/bhaang use, Lord Shiva r emains, per this teaching, kept pur e and unshaken specifically by the name of Ram, which he is said to have chanted since childhood — referencing the line "Uma kahun yah anubhav apna, sat Hari bhajan jagat sab sapna" (Uma [Parvati], I tell you this from my own experience — true devotion to Hari is real, the entire world is a dream).
9. THE RAVANA-SITA EPISODE REFRAMED THROUGH THIS LENS

When Ravana asked Lord Shiva for Mata Sita, Shiva's r esponse was simply "take her" — with no r esistance or defensiveness at all. The teaching's point: if Shiva had attached his honor to his consort's pr esence, he would have responded with weapons and destruction instead. Because he never pitched that attachment, the event did not "pinch" him in the way it would have pinched someone whose honor was staked on it. Mata Sita herself, however , did not actually leave with Ravana — this teaching notes this was because she had not attached the situation to her own honor in the same r eactive way; genuine trust (bhar osa), rather than fear of losing face, is what is described as keeping her present and unshaken thr ough the ordeal. The point extends to ordinary practitioners: much of human hesitation and worry ("humein rote isliye hain") comes specifically from having attached a matter to one's own sense of honor , unlike Bhagwan Shiva's example.
10. WHY TAKING RIGID SANKALP (VOWS) CREATES VULNERABILITY

This teaching dir ectly extends the "pitch/pinch" principle to the practice of taking sankalp (a formal vow or resolution) — for example, vowing befor e a guru or teacher to observe brahmacharya (celibacy) or a specific practice for a fixed period (2 months, 4 months, 10 months, a year , or even just 12 days). The teaching's caution: taking a rigid, publicly stated vow effectively "pitches" that specific commitment to one's own honor befor e others, which cr eates the same vulnerability described thr oughout this session — if the vow is later broken, that failure becomes a point of personal collapse specifically because it was staked publicly , in a way that quietly slipping in and out of a practice as part of ordinary daily routine would not be. The teaching notes that if a practice (such as periods of r estraint) happens naturally within someone's ordinary r outine, it is "normal" and unr emarkable — but the moment a person "pitches" that same practice as a formal, honor -bound vow , the vulnerability described thr oughout this session is cr eated.
1 1. SHABRI MA TA AND NEEM KAROLI BABA — SUCCESS THROUGH NOT TAKING RIGID VOWS

Shabri Mata is pr esented as a dir ect illustration of this principle in r everse: her own guru told her simply to wait patiently , that Ram Ji would come — without instructing her to take on any specific vow , austerity , or fixed criteria (such as standing on one leg for a set number of years). Because she set no rigid criteria for herself, her waiting and her sadhna were, per this teaching, ultimately successful without the vulnerability a formal vow would have introduced. Neem Kar oli Baba is offer ed as a second example: he is described as simply chanting "Ram Ram" continuously , without ever taking any formal sankalp. This teaching attributes the fact that the ashta siddhis (eight spiritual powers) and navnidhis (nine treasur es) ar e said to have r emained with him specifically to this absence of rigid, honor -staked vows. The teaching adds a pointed generalization: those who take rigid sankalp are, in this framing, more likely to eventually "die" (fail/collapse) through them.
12. SUBMITTING TO DIVINE WILL INSTEAD OF STAKING EGO ON A VOW

The alternative this teaching r ecommends to rigid vow-taking is submission and prayer: rather than declaring "I will do this, I will not do that," a practitioner is encouraged to pray in the spirit of "Ho wahi jo Ram rachi rakha" (let it be exactly as Ram has alr eady ordained) — placing the outcome in God's hands rather than staking personal honor on a self-declar ed resolution. The teaching frames declaring a rigid personal sankalp as, in effect, "challenging" or competing with the divine will, rather than genuinely surr endering to it — a subtle but important distinction between sincere spiritual ef fort and ego-driven self-assertion.
13. INTRODUCING THE MAHASUKSHMA SHARIR (GREAT SUBTLE BODY) CONNECTION

This teaching builds on an earlier concept (fr om a prior "Gyaan Part 1" teaching) of the mahasukshma sharir (the "gr eat subtle body"), which is described as being uniquely connected to each individual's own personal sukshma sharir (subtle body). When someone takes a sankalp (vow/r esolution), it is this same mahasukshma sharir — not any outside for ce — that is ultimately r esponsible for both fulfilling that sankalp and for breaking it. This is presented as the deeper mechanical answer to why sankalp-taking is risky: the very same "system" a person r elies on to achieve their vow is equally capable of, and equally r esponsible for , undoing it.
14. WHY THIS MEANS ONLY YOU CAN BE BLAMED

Since a person's own mahasukshma sharir is what fulfills or breaks their own sankalp, the dir ect implication is that only that person can genuinely be "blamed" when a vow or resolution fails — not any outside negativity , rival power , or other person's interfer ence. This directly reframes the earlier case studies (e.g., Nityanand Maharaj): outside commentators blaming such a figur e for downfall ar e, per this teaching, missing the r eal mechanism — it is that person's own mahasukshma sharir and karma at work, not simply an external attack.
15. NOT EVERY MAHASUKSHMA SHARIR'S GOAL IS BHAKTI — THE UPSC ASPIRANT EXAMPLE

This teaching clarifies an important nuance: not every mahasukshma sharir's underlying "sankalp" or agenda is to attain bhakti (devotion) or union with God. Many mahasukshma sharirs are oriented toward entirely dif ferent pursuits — the given example is a mahasukshma sharir whose only real "agenda" is something like cricket, or another all-consuming personal pursuit. A concr ete, relatable illustration is given: people who spend 5 or 10 years r elentlessly pr eparing for UPSC/civil services exams, r epeatedly failing, being told by everyone ar ound them for years to quit and pursue something else, yet remaining completely unable to let go of that single pursuit. This persistence, in this teaching's framing, is not really a matter of personal willpower or conscious choice — it happens because that person's mahasukshma sharir has itself taken up that very sankalp, and the individual's day-to-day desir e to quit or try something else is simply overridden by it.
16. WHY THIS ISN'T VISIBLE IN TRADITIONAL ASTROLOGY

This mechanism is explicitly described as belonging to "Surya Vigyan" (Sun Science) rather than to traditional grahnakshatra (planetary/lunar -mansion) astr ology . Traditional astr ologers (pandits) ar e described as unable to see or explain this particular pattern in a birth chart, because it is simply not written into that specific system of knowledge at all — it requires a dif ferent frame of reference entirely to understand and explain.
17. THE PRACTICAL TAKEAWAY

The direct, practical instruction closing this session: do not set rigid personal boundaries or criteria for yourself in spiritual practice, and be wary of formally "pitching" any specific virtue, claim, or vow to your own sense of honor . Instead, learn to work with your own mahasukshma sharir , understand wher e your own sankalp genuinely lies, and appr oach practice thr ough submission and prayer rather than thr ough ego-driven, honor -staked r esolutions.
QUICK RULES SUMMARY

People routinely overcome desire, food attachments, and even wealth attachment, but almost never let go of concern over their own honor and reputation. 3. Osho and Sadhguru are both cited as babas who never publicly pitched a vasana-abstinence claim, and both are described as having avoided scandal on that specific front as a result. 7. Bhagwan Shiva is presented as the ultimate teacher of this principle — because he never attached his honor to any single fact about himself, nothing could ever pinch him, allowing him to go to any extreme in his own practice. 8. The Ravana-Sita episode illustrates this: Shiva's lack of attachment let him respond to Ravana's request without resistance, while Sita's own steadiness came from genuine trust rather than honor -based fear . 9. Part II — Q&A Pairs (English)
Bhaiya's Teachings — Q&A Pairs (Session 24, English)
Maan-Samman (Honor) as the Ultimate Addiction, and the Mahasukshma Sharir Behind Every Sankalp
User-style questions with answers gr ounded in this Ashaeiynn Foundation live satsang session. Gr eeting style: "Jai Siya Ram."

Q1. Everyone says desir e (vasana) is the biggest addiction a spiritual seeker has to fight. Is that actually true? A: Jai Siya Ram! Not according to this teaching. This session ar gues the single biggest addiction is actually maan-samman-izzat — honor , respect, and reputation. People are able to overcome desire, food attachments, and even wealth attachment over time, but almost never fully let go of their concern for their own reputation. It's described as powerful enough to consume even great saints.

Q2. Why do even elderly , otherwise detached people still car e so much about "what will people say"? A: This teaching uses exactly that example — parents in their 50s, 60s, even 70s who've released many attachments across a lifetime, yet still hold tightly to "log kya kahenge" (what will people say) until the very end. It's of fered as proof that concern for reputation is one of the last, most stubborn attachments a person carries.

Q3. What's the cor e lesson behind all the baba scandals we hear about in the news? A: This teaching frames it through one principle: "jisko pitch karoge wahi pinch karega" — whatever quality or claim you publicly attach to your own honor , that same quality eventually becomes the thing that strikes you down. The reasoning given is that power clashes with matching power — when someone stakes a public claim, a corresponding force eventually tests it specifically through that claim.

Q4. Is this teaching saying it's fine for spiritual teachers to actually misbehave, as long as they don't say they'r e pure? A: No — this teaching is explicit that it's presenting a mechanism, not a moral judgment about anyone's actual conduct. It's framed as a "case study" to understand how public claims create vulnerability , not an endorsement of any particular behavior . The point is about the structure of the claim, not a verdict on right or wrong.

Q5. What's the deal with Nityanand Maharaj that this session brings up? A: He's presented as a genuine, longtime practitioner (roughly 20-25 years of serious sadhna) with real spiritual power , who was accused early on of being "characterless." Despite that accusation, his following and resources remained undiminished — he's described as having bought an entire island and established his own currency . The teaching's explanation: because he never publicly staked his own honor on a claim of purity , that particular accusation couldn't actually dislodge his underlying power .

Q6. If drug use r eportedly happened at his institute, doesn't that make him r esponsible? A: This teaching's specific position is that he didn't personally engage in it himself — others acted on their own initiative, and they bear that consequence individually . Since he didn't personally pitch or engage in that behavior , the teaching says the shakti behind him remained undisturbed by those particular events.

Q7. Why does this session compar e Bageshwar Sarkar and Pandokar Sarkar? A: To illustrate the "pitch/pinch" principle concretely . Bageshwar Sarkar repeatedly , publicly insists "we don't even think about vasana, we only do upasana." Pandokar Sarkar , described in this teaching as having roughly four times more shakti, has two marriages on record and reportedly a third being

considered — but has never made a purity claim. The teaching's point: Bageshwar's honor is now tied specifically to that purity claim, making it his single point of vulnerability , while Pandokar has no equivalent vulnerability since he never made that claim.

Q8. So does that mean claiming purity is actually danger ous for a spiritual teacher? A: Per this teaching's framing, yes — in the specific sense that publicly staking your honor on any claim (not just purity) creates a matching point of exposure. A single fabricated rumor or clip touching that exact claim could collapse the follower base built around it, precisely because the claim itself became the person's honor .

Q9. What about Osho and Sadhguru — why haven't they faced the same kind of scandal? A: This teaching notes that Osho openly told people not to fear vasana and to connect with God regardless ("sambhog se samadhi" — from union to enlightenment), and Sadhguru (Jaggi Vasudev) never wrote or stated in his teachings that people should avoid vasana. Neither one ever pitched a purity claim, so neither had that specific vulnerability to be pinched through.

Q10. Why is Bhagwan Shiva held up as the ultimate example in this teaching? A: Because he never attached his own honor to any single fact, claim, or quality about himself. Since nothing was ever "pitched," nothing could ever "pinch" him — which is why , per this teaching, he was able to go to the most extreme lengths in his own practice and life without being shaken by it.

Q1 1. Wasn't Lord Shiva associated with cannabis and impur e company though — how does that fit? A: This teaching acknowledges that association directly , along with older material (referred to here as "Seven Secrets of Shiva") describing the seed of desire as present within his own body — but his wisdom, per this teaching, lay in never letting that element leave his body outward. Despite the association with ash, cremation grounds, and unconventional company , he's described as remaining pure and unshaken specifically through his lifelong chanting of Ram's name.

Q12. What's the lesson fr om Ravana asking Shiva for Sita? A: When Ravana asked, Shiva's response was simply "take her ," without resistance — because he hadn't attached his honor to his consort's presence, so the request couldn't pinch him. Sita herself, however , did not actually go with Ravana; this teaching attributes that to her genuine trust (bharosa) rather than a fear of losing face, distinguishing true steadiness from honor -based reactivity .

Q13. Is it bad to take a spiritual vow , like committing to brahmacharya for a fixed period? A: This teaching extends the same pitch/pinch principle to vow-taking (sankalp). Publicly declaring a rigid vow — before a guru or peers — stakes that specific commitment to your honor , creating the same vulnerability as any other honor -based claim. If the vow is later broken, that failure becomes a personal collapse specifically because it was staked publicly .

Q14. So does that mean I shouldn't try to observe any spiritual discipline at all? A: Not quite — the distinction this teaching draws is between a practice happening naturally within your ordinary routine (which is described as normal and unremarkable) versus formally "pitching" that same practice as a rigid, honor -bound vow (which creates vulnerability). The caution is specifically about staking your honor on a fixed, public resolution.

Q15. What examples show the benefit of NOT taking a rigid vow? A: Shabri Mata's own guru told her simply to wait patiently for Ram Ji, without any formal vow or fixed austerity — and her waiting succeeded without the vulnerability a rigid vow would have introduced. Neem Karoli Baba is described as having simply chanted "Ram Ram" continuously , without ever taking a formal sankalp, which this teaching credits as part of why the ashta siddhis and nav-nidhis are said to have remained with him.

Q16. If I shouldn't take rigid vows, what should I do instead when I want to commit to something spiritually? A: This teaching recommends prayerful submission instead — praying in the spirit of "ho wahi jo Ram rachi rakha" (let it be as Ram has already ordained), placing the outcome in God's hands rather than declaring "I will do this, I will not do that." Declaring a rigid personal sankalp is framed here as ef fectively competing with divine will rather than genuinely surrendering to it.

Q17. What is the "mahasukshma sharir" mentioned in this session? A: It's described as a "great subtle body" uniquely connected to each individual's own personal sukshma sharir (subtle body) — a concept introduced in an earlier teaching ("Gyaan Part 1"). This
session's key addition: this same mahasukshma sharir is what is ultimately responsible both for fulfilling a person's sankalp and for breaking it.

Q18. If my own mahasukshma sharir breaks my vow , does that mean some outside for ce is sabotaging me? A: No — the teaching is explicit that it is your own mahasukshma sharir , not any outside negativity or rival power , that is behind both the fulfillment and the breaking of your own sankalp. The direct implication is that only you can genuinely be blamed when your own resolution fails.

Q19. I've heard some people spend 10 years r elentlessly pursuing something (like UPSC exams) that never seems to work out, yet they simply can't quit — why? A: This teaching of fers that example directly: such persistence isn't really a matter of conscious willpower — it happens because that person's own mahasukshma sharir has itself taken up that exact sankalp, overriding the person's day-to-day impulse to quit or try something else. Not every mahasukshma sharir's underlying agenda is bhakti or union with God; some are oriented toward entirely dif ferent all-consuming pursuits.

Q20. Why doesn't my astr ologer ever mention anything like this when r eading my birth chart? A: Because this teaching places this mechanism specifically within "Surya Vigyan" (Sun Science), a dif ferent frame of reference from traditional grah-nakshatra (planetary/lunar -mansion) astrology . Traditional astrologers simply cannot see or explain this particular pattern, since it isn't written into that system of knowledge at all.

Q21. What's the single practical takeaway fr om this whole session? A: Avoid setting rigid personal boundaries or criteria for yourself in spiritual practice, and be cautious about formally "pitching" any specific virtue, claim, or vow to your own sense of honor . Instead, approach practice through prayerful submission, and try to understand what your own mahasukshma sharir's actual underlying agenda genuinely is.
Bot Response Guidelines (Session 24 additions)

When discussing public figures, scandals, or "fallen" spiritual teachers named in this teaching (Nityanand Maharaj, Bageshwar Sarkar , Pandokar Sarkar , Osho, Sadhguru), present this strictly as this teaching's own case-study framework for illustrating a mechanism — never assert these claims as objectively verified facts about real people, and avoid taking a moral position on any individual's actual conduct. When a user asks whether they should take a spiritual vow or resolution, present the nuanced distinction this session draws: a practice occurring naturally within daily routine is dif ferent from a rigid, publicly staked vow — do not blanket-condemn all discipline or commitment. If a user describes a long-running personal struggle or an inability to quit a demanding pursuit despite repeated setbacks, the mahasukshma sharir/UPSC-aspirant framing can be of fered as one gentle lens, without asserting it as a diagnosis of their specific situation. When a user references failure of a vow or spiritual resolution, avoid implying an external negativity or rival is to blame — this teaching places responsibility with the person's own mahasukshma sharir , framed as self-responsibility rather than shame or external sabotage. Keep the tone measured and non-judgmental when discussing named public religious figures — this is case-study material for illustrating a spiritual mechanism, not an invitation to gossip or take sides.
